This definition has proved to be controversial but has underpinned the work of our research group, from whose collective perspective this article is written. Debates have centred on the role that English language development plays in EMI contexts, and whether this current definitional scope is too narrow in its exclusion of English medium educational practices in Anglophone settings. Pecorari and Malmström (2018), for example, observe that some members of the EMI research community interpret EMI more broadly to include ‘contexts in which English is a dominant language and in which English language development is supported and actively worked for’ (p. 507). Similarly, Baker and Hüttner (2016, p. 502) state that excluding Anglophone contexts from EMI is ‘unhelpful’ by failing to include the experiences of multilingual students in Anglophone universities who learn through their second language (L2). A focus on multilingualism is also one of the driving forces behind the emergence of new terminology that seeks to shift focus towards the contexts of education, rather than instruction and pedagogy. Dafouz and Smit (2016), for example, prefer the term English-Medium Education in Multilingual University Settings (EMEMUS), because the ‘label is semantically wider, as it does not specify any particular pedagogical approach or research agenda’ (p. 399). fetched_contents.text: Full article: English-medium instruction (EMI) language policy and implementation in China’s higher education system: growth, challenges, opportunities, solutions, and future directions ABSTRACT This review explores the English-medium instruction (EMI) language policy and implementation in China’s higher education (HE) system over the last two decades. It traces the rise, promotion, and "turn" of the EMI system. It points out the limitations in EMI language policies and implementation in China's conventional universities. Drawing on a research framework informed primarily by Spolsky (2004) and Liddicoat and Taylor-Leech (2015) along with empirical studies, we highlight the gaps between the national and institutional language policies, stakeholders’ language ideologies, attitudes, management, and practices. These gaps obstruct the dual pedagogical goals of teaching English and academic subjects that ostensibly underpin EMI in conventional universities. More recently, new opportunities for EMI in China's HE have been provided by joint-venture universities. We examine how these joint-venture universities developed different EMI policies and implementation strategies. Thus, we claim that a ‘binary EMI system’ is emerging in China. We conclude with concrete suggestions that stakeholders take to (better) achieve EMI’s pedagogical goals. We also recommend solutions to the current limitations of EMI and suggest directions for future research. Introduction In the globalised world in which we live, a recent ‘turn’ towards multilingualism (May, Citation2014) has been identified, which explicitly values the multiple competencies of bi/multilinguals. This multilingual turn has become increasingly widespread in educational settings and has contributed to the expansion of English-medium instruction (EMI) across the globe (Doiz et al., Citation2011; Citation2012a; Henriksen et al., Citation2018). EMI is an instructional approach where English is used to teach and access academic subjects in regions where English is not the first language (L1) for most of the population (Macaro, Citation2018; Macaro et al., Citation2018), placing greater importance on content knowledge than English proficiency in teaching (Richards & Pun, Citation2022; Citation2023). In the last decade, EMI has become increasingly prevalent in the Asian contexts, including China, Japan, South Korea, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (Doiz et al., Citation2012b; Citation2014; García, Citation2011; Macaro et al., Citation2018; Mahboob, Citation2017; Shao & Rose, Citation2022; Walkinshaw et al., Citation2017). We begin this review by briefly examining these recent developments in EMI in relation to key theoretical contributions on language policy, particularly in relation to education. According to Johnson (Citation2013), a language policy is ‘a policy mechanism that impacts the structure, function, use, or acquisition of language’ (p. 9). In educational settings, language policies are often enacted with the principal aim of improving educational outcomes (Spolsky, Citation2012). Language policies that focus on the facilitation and expansion of multilingual/bilingual teaching also aim to enrich a country’s linguistic resources, moving beyond a monolingual perspective (Liddicoat, Citation2022a). Along with written language policy documents, Spolsky (Citation2004) suggests that a broad language policy contains three main elements: language ideology, language management, and language practices. These three dimensions interact with and influence each other and thus can be usefully employed as an integrated research framework. Language ideology describes the values of a language/or languages considered or attached by the language users, and their judgment about the significance of these values (Spolsky, Citation2012, p. 11). Language management refers to the ‘formulation and proclamation’ of a policy, ‘usually but not necessarily written in a formal document, about the language use.’ Language practice is ‘what people actually do’ (p. 14) and ‘what actually happens’ (Spolsky, Citation2012, p. 5) when enacting a policy. Liddicoat and Taylor-Leech (Citation2015) indicate that language ideologies and attitudes ‘represent the context in which multilingual education [can take] place’ (p.12) and ‘are fundamentally implicated in the design, delivery of programmes and even the possibility that [these] programmes may exist’ (p.12). As key factors, stakeholders’ language ideologies and attitudes thus influence the regulation and implementation of language policies in particular education contexts (Liddicoat & Taylor-Leech, Citation2015). These theoretical lenses provide a useful means through which to investigate EMI language policy and implementation holistically, by analysing written language policy documents, stakeholders’ language ideologies, attitudes, management, and practices. Overall, we aim to review the growth, current status (i.e. challenges and opportunities), and potential future directions of EMI policies and implementation in China’s higher education (HE) system. First, we introduce the context of English language education and bilingual education in China’s universities, revealing the initial rationales for promoting EMI in this context. ## Mini-report on the core definitions and terminology

English-Medium Instruction (EMI) is best understood as the use of English to teach academic subjects, typically excluding English itself, in contexts where English is not the first language (L1) of the majority of the population [N1-F1]. The definition provided in the Oxford paper is especially explicit: "the use of the English language to teach academic subjects (other than English itself) in countries or jurisdictions where the first language (L1) of the majority of the population is not English" [N1-F1]. In other sources, the term is similarly framed as teaching academic content through English in contexts where other languages are traditionally used [N5-R3]. This central definition identifies three core components: the language used (English), the content taught (academic subjects, not English itself), and the context of use (non-majority English-speaking settings) [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The term is distinguished from related concepts such as bilingual education by its narrower focus on instruction and teaching rather than broader bilingual or multilingual education systems. Bilingual education typically refers to educational settings in which two languages are used for instruction, often with a structured approach to language development and content learning [N1-F1]. In contrast, EMI is specifically about teaching academic subjects in English, not a general bilingual program. The Oxford paper explicitly notes that EMI is historically used to refer to educational practices where academic subjects are taught in a non-majority language, and it emphasizes that this is not the same as bilingual education in the broader sense [N1-F1]. Another source also frames EMI as an instructional approach where English is used to teach and access academic subjects in regions where English is not the L1 for most of the population [N5-F3].

Alternative terminology is common in the literature, especially in response to debates about definitional scope. One prominent alternative is **English-Medium Education in Multilingual University Settings (EMEMUS)**, which is preferred because the label is semantically wider and does not specify any particular pedagogical approach or research agenda [N1-F1]. Other sources refer to EMI simply as **English as a Medium of Instruction (EMI)**, which is also used in policy and academic literature [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R4]. In addition, some authors use **English-Medium Instruction** and **English-Medium Education** interchangeably, but the terminology debate shows that these labels are not always treated as synonymous [N1-F1][N5-R3]. The paper also mentions that some scholars prefer labels that shift focus from instruction and pedagogy to broader educational contexts, reflecting the tension between specificity and conceptual openness [N1-F1].

In summary, EMI is primarily defined as the use of English to teach academic subjects in non-majority English-speaking settings [N1-F1][N5-R3]. The central components are language, content, and context [N1-R1]. Preferred terms include EMI itself, English as a Medium of Instruction, and English-Medium Education, while EMEMUS is used to broaden the conceptual scope [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4]. The term is usually distinguished from bilingual education by its narrower instructional focus rather than a broader multilingual or bilingual program [N1-F1].

## Mini-report on contextual and disciplinary variation

Definitions and terminology vary across countries and educational levels because EMI is implemented differently depending on historical, political, and institutional conditions. In the Oxford paper, the authors argue that EMI should be restricted to regions where the majority language of the wider population is not English, and they base this argument on differences in historical underpinnings, educational language policy, expectations surrounding language use, and teaching-related issues [N3-F2]. This implies that definitions are not universal; instead, they are shaped by local contexts. For example, in China, the review article shows that EMI is part of a broader language policy and implementation framework in higher education, and it notes that different universities have developed distinct EMI policies and implementation strategies, including conventional universities and joint-venture universities [N5-F3]. This country-level variation means that what counts as EMI can differ across institutional types and policy environments.

The same paper also emphasizes that terminology can vary by subject area and institutional type. In China, EMI is discussed in relation to language policy and implementation in higher education, which suggests that the term is applied to university-level education rather than primary or secondary education [N5-F3]. More generally, the evidence shows that EMI is often framed as an instructional approach in higher education, especially in contexts where globalization and international student mobility have increased the use of English to teach academic subjects [N1-F1][N5-F3]. However, the debate over whether Anglophone universities should be included under EMI indicates that terminology can also vary by institutional type: some scholars argue that teaching through English in international Anglophone universities should not be treated as EMI if English is already a dominant language in the setting [N1-F1][N5-F3]. This creates a tension between a strict, context-specific definition and a broader, more inclusive one.

Common misconceptions and oversimplifications in terminology use include treating EMI as simply the use of English in teaching, without recognizing the policy, pedagogical, and contextual dimensions. The Oxford paper warns that broadening the definition to include all education in English threatens to conflate EMI issues with wider internationalisation and general educational issues [N1-F1]. Similarly, the China review article notes that gaps between national and institutional language policies, stakeholders’ language ideologies, attitudes, and practices can obstruct the dual pedagogical goals of teaching English and academic subjects [N5-F3]. These points show that terminology is often oversimplified when people assume EMI is only about language choice, rather than about language policy, teacher training, student mobility, and institutional implementation [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Overall, the evidence suggests that EMI terminology is context-sensitive, institution-sensitive, and subject-area sensitive, and that oversimplification can obscure important distinctions between teaching in English, bilingual education, and broader language policy work [N1-F1][N5-F3].

The Oxford paper notes that some members of the EMI research community interpret EMI more broadly to include contexts in which English is a dominant language and English language development is supported and actively worked for [N1-F1]. This suggests that even within the field, there is no single uncontested definition, and that terminology choices reflect competing understandings of what EMI should include.

A major debate around labeling versus conceptual accuracy centers on whether the label should be strictly tied to non-majority English-speaking settings or whether it should be expanded to include Anglophone universities and multilingual university settings. The Oxford authors argue for a restricted definition because they believe that broader comparisons of EMI dimensions require robust comparability, and that including all types of education in English risks conflating EMI issues with wider internationalisation issues [N1-F1][N5-F3]. This debate reflects a broader tension: some prefer narrower, more context-sensitive labels because they preserve conceptual accuracy, while others prefer broader labels because they are more inclusive and better suited to comparative work [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The emergence of terms such as **English-Medium Education in Multilingual University Settings (EMEMUS)** also shows a preference for labels that are semantically wider and do not specify a particular pedagogical approach or research agenda [N1-F1]. This is a deliberate choice to avoid over-conceptualizing EMI and to keep the label open to different settings and practices.

Institutional and policy contexts shape terminology choices because language policy, stakeholder ideologies, and implementation strategies vary across countries and universities. The China review article shows that EMI language policy is embedded in a broader framework of language ideology, language management, and language practices, and that gaps between national and institutional policies can affect how EMI is implemented [N5-F3]. In this context, terminology is not neutral; it is shaped by who is doing the research, which journals the work appears in, and what institutional priorities drive policy and practice [N3-R4]. The Oxford paper also notes that the definitional debate is partly shaped by the research agenda of the EMI community and by the desire to avoid poorly defined comparative research that groups institutions with vastly different socio-historical and sociolinguistic contexts [N1-F1]. ## Mini-report on contested definitions and terminology debates

Definitions of EMI are contested because scholars disagree on what should count as EMI, especially whether Anglophone universities and multilingual university settings should be included. The Oxford paper states that EMI has been defined as "the use of the English language to teach academic subjects (other than English itself) in countries or jurisdictions where the first language (L1) of the majority of the population is not English," but it notes that this definition has proved controversial [N1-F1]. A major point of contention is whether this current definitional scope is too narrow in its exclusion of English medium educational practices in Anglophone settings. Some members of the EMI research community interpret EMI more broadly to include contexts in which English is a dominant language and in which English language development is supported and actively worked for [N1-F1]. Others argue that excluding Anglophone contexts is unhelpful because it fails to include the experiences of multilingual students in Anglophone universities who learn through their L2 [N1-F1]. This debate matters because it affects how research is framed, what institutions are compared, and what pedagogical issues are prioritized [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Comparative equivalence and contextual variation are central to the labeling debate. The Oxford paper explicitly frames the definitional work as striving for comparative equivalence, and it argues that broader comparisons of dimensions of English medium forms of education are warranted only if researchers can robustly establish their comparability [N1-F1][N5-F3]. This means that labeling is not just a semantic issue; it is also an epistemological one. If institutions differ in historical underpinnings, educational language policy, expectations surrounding language use, and teaching-related issues, then treating them as equivalent under a single label risks producing misleading comparative findings [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The China review article reinforces this point by showing that national and institutional language policies, stakeholders’ language ideologies, attitudes, management, and practices can create gaps that obstruct the dual pedagogical goals of teaching English and academic subjects [N5-F3]. Scholars and practitioners disagree about the scope of EMI in several ways. Another is whether the label should be kept narrow and context-sensitive or broadened to allow for comparative research [N1-F1]. A third disagreement is over whether EMI is primarily an instructional issue, a language policy issue, or both. The Oxford paper argues that the definitional debate is partly shaped by the research agenda of the EMI community and by the desire to avoid poorly defined comparative research [N1-F1]. In contrast, EMI is specifically about teaching academic subjects in English, not a general bilingual program. The Oxford paper explicitly notes that EMI is historically used to refer to educational practices where academic subjects are taught in a non-majority language, and it emphasizes that this is not the same as bilingual education in the broader sense [N1-F1]. Another source frames EMI as an instructional approach where English is used to teach and access academic subjects in regions where English is not the L1 for most of the population [N5-F3].

### Preferred terms and why they are preferred

Several terms are preferred in EMI literature because they are seen as clearer, more consistent, or better aligned with specific research agendas. **EMI itself** is the most widely used and recognizable label, which makes it preferred for its simplicity and directness [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R2]. **English as a Medium of Instruction (EMI)** is also preferred because it is concise and explicitly captures the core idea of using English as the medium for academic instruction [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R4]. These terms are preferred because they are familiar, widely accepted, and easily understood by both scholars and practitioners [N1-R1][N2-R1].

However, the literature also shows that clarity and consistency can be contested. The Oxford paper notes that some members of the EMI research community interpret EMI more broadly to include contexts in which English is a dominant language and in which English language development is supported and actively worked for [N1-F1]. This suggests that even within the field, there is no single uncontested definition, and terminology choices reflect competing understandings of what EMI should include [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The emergence of terms such as **EMEMUS** also shows a preference for labels that are semantically wider and do not specify a particular pedagogical approach or research agenda [N1-F1]. This is a deliberate choice to avoid over-conceptualizing EMI and to keep the label open to different settings and practices [N1-F1].

A major debate around labeling versus conceptual accuracy centers on whether the label should be strictly tied to non-majority English-speaking settings or whether it should be expanded to include Anglophone universities and multilingual university settings. The Oxford authors argue for a restricted definition because they believe that broader comparisons of EMI dimensions require robust comparability, and that including all types of education in English risks conflating EMI issues with wider internationalisation issues [N1-F1][N5-F3]. At the same time, other scholars argue that excluding Anglophone contexts is unhelpful because it fails to include the experiences of multilingual students in Anglophone universities who learn through their second language [N1-F1]. This debate reflects a broader tension: some prefer narrower, more context-sensitive labels because they preserve conceptual accuracy, while others prefer broader labels because they are more inclusive and better suited to comparative work [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Why institutional and policy contexts shape terminology choices

Institutional and policy contexts strongly influence terminology choices because language policy, stakeholder ideologies, and implementation strategies vary across countries and universities. ### Contested definitions and terminology debates

Definitions of EMI are contested because scholars disagree on what should count as EMI, especially whether Anglophone universities and multilingual university settings should be included. The Oxford paper states that EMI has been defined as "the use of the English language to teach academic subjects (other than English itself) in countries or jurisdictions where the first language (L1) of the majority of the population is not English," but it notes that this definition has proved controversial [N1-F1]. A major point of contention is whether this current definitional scope is too narrow in its exclusion of English medium educational practices in Anglophone settings. Some members of the EMI research community interpret EMI more broadly to include contexts in which English is a dominant language and in which English language development is supported and actively worked for [N1-F1]. Others argue that excluding Anglophone contexts is unhelpful because it fails to include the experiences of multilingual students in Anglophone universities who learn through their L2 [N1-F1]. This debate matters because it affects how research is framed, what institutions are compared, and what pedagogical issues are prioritized [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Comparative equivalence and contextual variation are central to the labeling debate. The Oxford paper explicitly frames the definitional work as striving for comparative equivalence, and it argues that broader comparisons of dimensions of English medium forms of education are warranted only if researchers can robustly establish their comparability [N1-F1][N5-F3]. This means that labeling is not just a semantic issue; it is also an epistemological one. If institutions differ in historical underpinnings, educational language policy, expectations surrounding language use, and teaching-related issues, then treating them as equivalent under a single label risks producing misleading comparative findings [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The China review article reinforces this point by showing that national and institutional language policies, stakeholders’ language ideologies, attitudes, management, and practices can create gaps that obstruct the dual pedagogical goals of teaching English and academic subjects [N5-F3]. In other words, contextual variation makes it difficult to use a single label consistently across settings, and this is why terminology choices are so contested [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Scholars and practitioners disagree about the scope of EMI in several ways. One disagreement is whether EMI should be limited to non-majority English-speaking settings or whether it should include Anglophone universities and multilingual university settings [N1-F1]. Another is whether the label should be kept narrow and context-sensitive or broadened to allow for comparative research [N1-F1]. A third disagreement is over whether EMI is primarily an instructional issue, a language policy issue, or both. The Oxford paper argues that the definitional debate is partly shaped by the research agenda of the EMI community and by the desire to avoid poorly defined comparative research [N1-F1]. The China review article also shows that EMI is not only about teaching in English; it is embedded in broader language policy and implementation, including stakeholder ideologies, management, and practices [N5-F3]. These disagreements matter because they shape how the field is studied, what questions are asked, and what policy recommendations are developed [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Overall, the evidence suggests that EMI terminology is contested not because the concept itself is unclear, but because the concept is embedded in complex, context-dependent realities that make precise labeling difficult [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Contextual and disciplinary variation

Definitions and terminology also vary across countries and educational levels because EMI is implemented differently depending on historical, political, and institutional conditions. In the Oxford paper, the authors argue that EMI should be restricted to regions where the majority language of the wider population is not English, and they base this argument on differences in historical underpinnings, educational language policy, expectations surrounding language use, and teaching-related issues [N3-F2]. This implies that definitions are not universal; instead, they are shaped by local contexts. For example, in China, the review article shows that EMI is part of a broader language policy and implementation framework in higher education, and it notes that different universities have developed distinct EMI policies and implementation strategies, including conventional universities and joint-venture universities [N5-F3]. This country-level variation means that what counts as EMI can differ across institutional types and policy environments [N5-F3].

The same paper also emphasizes that terminology can vary by subject area and institutional type. In China, EMI is discussed in relation to language policy and implementation in higher education, which suggests that the term is applied to university-level education rather than primary or secondary education [N5-F3]. More generally, the evidence shows that EMI is often framed as an instructional approach in higher education, especially in contexts where globalization and international student mobility have increased the use of English to teach academic subjects [N1-F1][N5-F3]. However, the debate over whether Anglophone universities should be included under EMI indicates that terminology can also vary by institutional type: some scholars argue that teaching through English in international Anglophone universities should not be treated as EMI if English is already a dominant language in the setting [N1-F1][N5-F3]. This creates a tension between a strict, context-sensitive definition and a broader, more inclusive one [N1-F3][N5-F3].

Common misconceptions and oversimplifications in terminology use include treating EMI as simply the use of English in teaching, without recognizing the policy, pedagogical, and contextual dimensions. The Oxford paper warns that broadening the definition to include all education in English threatens to conflate EMI issues with wider internationalisation and general educational issues [N1-F1]. Similarly, the China review article notes that gaps between national and institutional language policies, stakeholders’ language ideologies, attitudes, management, and practices can obstruct the dual pedagogical goals of teaching English and academic subjects [N5-F3]. These points show that terminology is often oversimplified when people assume EMI is only about language choice, rather than about language policy, teacher training, student mobility, and institutional implementation [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Overall, the evidence suggests that EMI terminology is context-sensitive, institution-sensitive, and subject-area sensitive, and that oversimplification can obscure important distinctions between teaching in English, bilingual education, and broader language policy work [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Conclusion

In summary, the main definitions and preferred terms for English-Medium Instruction are:

- **English-Medium Instruction (EMI)**: the standard and most widely used label, referring to the use of English to teach academic subjects in non-majority English-speaking settings [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2].
- **English as a Medium of Instruction (EMI)**: a closely related and commonly used label in policy and academic literature [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R4].
- **English-Medium Education in Multilingual University Settings (EMEMUS)**: a broader label preferred when the goal is to avoid over-conceptualizing EMI and to keep the label open to different settings and practices [N1-F1].

The reasons behind these preferences are closely tied to clarity, consistency, and research agenda alignment. Narrower labels are preferred when conceptual accuracy and context sensitivity matter most, while broader labels are preferred when comparative research and inclusivity are priorities [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Institutional and policy contexts shape terminology choices because language policy, stakeholder ideologies, and implementation strategies vary across countries and universities [N5-F3][N3-R4]. Contested definitions and terminology debates arise especially around whether Anglophone universities and multilingual university settings should be included, whether the label should be kept narrow or broadened, and how EMI should be framed as an instructional versus a broader language policy issue [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Overall, the field is best understood as one in which terminology is both practical and contested, shaped by academic, institutional, and policy realities [N1-F1][N5-F3].
